<meta>continues from previous page: the account of the domestic conflict involving Ping-er</meta>

<note>Patience <term>Ping-er</term>, a trusted maid, is seeking medicine after a violent incident.</note>
"They used the boards and sticks backwards, and while she just stood there, he grabbed something—I do not know what—and gave her a beating, breaking the skin on her face in two places. We heard that your Ladyship <note>referring to Aunt Xue</note> has a certain medicine here for staff-wounds; would you find a pill for me, Miss?"

When <term>Baochai</term> <gloss>Precious Virtue</gloss> heard this, she quickly ordered <term>Ying-er</term> <gloss>Oriole</gloss> to find two pills and give them to <term>Ping-er</term>. <term>Baochai</term> said, "Since that is the case, go and give her my regards; I will not go myself." <term>Ping-er</term> assented to <term>Baochai</term> and departed. This matter requires no further mention.

Now, after <term>Xiangling</term> <gloss>Fragrant Water-lily</gloss> had met everyone and finished dinner, <term>Baochai</term> and the others went to Grandmother Jia’s quarters. <term>Xiangling</term> took the opportunity to come to the <term>Xiaoxiang Guan</term> <gloss>Naiad’s House/瀟湘館</gloss>. By this time, <term>Daiyu</term> <gloss>Black Jade</gloss> was mostly recovered. Seeing <term>Xiangling</term> moving into the garden to live, she was naturally pleased. <term>Xiangling</term> said with a smile, "Now that I have come in here and have some free time, if you would somehow teach me how to compose poetry, it would be my great good fortune!" <term>Daiyu</term> smiled and replied, "Since you want to learn poetry, you must take me as your master. Although I am not truly proficient, I can generally manage to teach you." <term>Xiangling</term> laughed, "If that is really so, I shall take you as my master; you must not grow weary of me." 

<term>Daiyu</term> said, "What difficulty is there in it that makes it so worthy of study? It is nothing more than the <term>Qi, Cheng, Zhuan, He</term> <gloss>the four steps of a poem: introduction, development, transition, and conclusion</gloss>. Within the development and transition, there are two pairs of couplets: level tones against oblique tones, empty words against solid words, and solid against empty. If you truly have a brilliant line, it does not even matter if the tones and categories do not match perfectly."

<term>Xiangling</term> smiled, "No wonder I often steal a moment to look at a poem or two in an old book; some are perfectly matched, while others are not. I have also heard it said, 'the first, third, and fifth syllables do not matter, but the second, fourth, and sixth must be distinct.' Looking at the poems of the ancients, some follow this, but some are wrong on the second, fourth, or sixth syllables. I have been puzzled every day. Now hearing you speak, it turns out these rules are actually of no consequence, as long as the phrasing is novel and extraordinary."

<term>Daiyu</term> said, "That is exactly the principle. Phrasing is, after all, a secondary matter; the most important thing is the 'conception' <note>the underlying idea or intent</note>. If the intent and interest are genuine, then even without polishing the phrasing, it will naturally be good. This is called 'not letting the words damage the meaning.'"

<term>Xiangling</term> said, "I only love <term>Lu Fangweng</term>’s <note>the poet Lu You, 1125–1210</note> lines: 'The heavy curtains are not rolled up, keeping the fragrance long; the old inkstone is slightly concave, gathering much ink.' It is so vivid and interesting!"

<term>Daiyu</term> replied, "You must absolutely not look at such poetry. Because you do not yet understand poetry, you see something shallow and accessible and love it. Once you enter that mold, you will never be able to learn your way out of it. Just listen to me: if you truly wish to learn, I have here the <term>Complete Works of Wang Moji</term> <note>Wang Wei, the Tang dynasty 'Poet-Buddha'</note>. Take his one hundred five-character regulated poems and study them with careful deliberation until they are thoroughly familiar. Then read one hundred and twenty of Old <term>Du</term>’s <note>Du Fu, the 'Poet-Sage'</note> seven-character regulated poems. Next, read one or two hundred of <term>Li Qinglian</term>’s <note>Li Bai, the 'Poet-Immortal'</note> seven-character quatrains. Once you have these three men as your foundation, you can then take a look at <term>Tao Yuanming</term>, <term>Ying</term>, <term>Liu</term>, <term>Xie</term>, <term>Ruan</term>, <term>Yu</term>, and <term>Bao</term> <note>a list of classical poets from the Han, Wei, and Six Dynasties periods</note>. Since you are such an extremely clever and sharp person, in less than a year’s work, you need not worry about not becoming a true poet!" 

Hearing this, <term>Xiangling</term> smiled, "If it is like that, good sister, please take the book out for me. I will take it back and it would be good to read a few poems at night." Hearing this, <term>Daiyu</term> ordered <term>Zijuan</term> <gloss>Nightingale</gloss> to bring the five-character regulated poems of <term>Wang Youcheng</term> <note>another name for Wang Wei</note> and handed them to <term>Xiangling</term>, saying, "Only look at those with red circles; those are the ones I have selected. Read them one by one. If there is something you do not understand, ask your mistress <note>Baochai</note>, or if you happen to see me, I will explain it to you."

<term>Xiangling</term> took the poems and returned to the <term>Hengwu Yuan</term> <gloss>Alcaic Enclosure/蘅蕪院</gloss>. Ignoring all other matters, she began to read them one by one under the lamp. <term>Baochai</term> urged her to go to sleep several times, but she would not. Seeing her such devotion, <term>Baochai</term> had no choice but to leave her to it.

One day, just as <term>Daiyu</term> had finished washing and dressing, she saw <term>Xiangling</term> coming with the book, beaming with smiles, wanting to exchange it for <term>Du</term>’s regulated poems. <term>Daiyu</term> smiled and asked, "How many poems do you remember in total?" <term>Xiangling</term> laughed, "I have read all of those marked with red circles." <term>Daiyu</term> said, "Have you gained any insight yet?" <term>Xiangling</term> smiled, "I have indeed gained some insight, but I do not know if it is correct. Let me tell it to you."

<summary>Xiangling begins her formal apprenticeship in poetry under Daiyu's tutelage. Daiyu provides a curriculum focused on Tang masters like Wang Wei, Du Fu, and Li Bai, emphasizing that poetic intent is more important than rigid formal rules.</summary>
<keywords>Xiangling, Daiyu, Baochai, poetry education, Wang Wei, Du Fu, Li Bai, regulated verse, Tang Dynasty poetry, Xiaoxiang Guan</keywords>
